History will judge this war not by what Trump destroyed in Iran, but by what it leaves behind: the fate of the regime, its nuclear program, its missiles and proxies—and its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. @AC360 with @brett_mcgurk @CedricLeighton

Video

Remarkable reporting on how and why Trump decided to go to war with Iran—the first draft of history, by @maggieNYT and @jonathanvswan.


Maggie Haberman (@maggieNYT)

HOW TRUMP TOOK THE US TO WAR WITH IRAN: @jonathanvswan and report for our forthcoming book, out June 23 with excerpt here nytimes.com/2026/04/07/us/po…




— https://nitter.net/maggieNYT/status/2041571583228043640#m

Trump's threats to destroy Iranian civilization are a gift to the regime. They will alienate even its fiercest opponents, who believe the Islamic Republic has spent decades erasing 2500 years of Iranian civilization. It's malpractice for the U.S. president to threaten the same.


Jake Tapper 🦅 (@jaketapper)

The president of the United States, 8:06 am ET, threatens Iran: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.“





— https://nitter.net/jaketapper/status/204149289

6 Trump is measuring this war not by what it will achieve but by what it has destroyed. Ordinary Iranians are now navigating two hells: a cruel regime that has spent half a century repressing them, and a war that is deepening their despair rather than relieving it.

5 Trump has abandoned his own rationale in Iran. This war was ostensibly launched to aid Iranians massacred by their own government. Now he's threatening to destroy their civilization. theatlantic.com/internationa…

4 Trump is hoping for a partner in Tehran, but Ayatollah Khamenei spent decades selecting men whose identity depended on ideological fealty to the revolution. The Islamic Republic now resembles a ship with neither a captain able to turn the wheel nor a crew willing to let him.

3 As a former real-estate developer, Trump seemingly has no mental framework for this adversary. In real estate, both sides want a transaction. The U.S.-Iran conflict is not a transaction but a cold war in which one side fears normalization more than continued conflict.

2 The carrots that America offers the nation—normalization and reintegration--are sticks to the men who rule it. And the sticks that America wields against the regime—destruction and isolation—are carrots to men whose power depends on both. nitter.net/BBCBreaking/status/204…


BBC Breaking News (@BBCBreaking)

Donald Trump says "a whole civilisation will die tonight" if Iran fails to make deal - follow live bbc.in/3PLAa5D




— https://nitter.net/BBCBreaking/status/2041493580636652025#m

1 The Islamic Republic operates under a survival paradox: What makes the regime thrive makes the nation suffer, and what the nation needs to thrive threatens the regime’s survival. My @TheAtlantic essay on how Trump misreads his adversary.  theatlantic.com/internationa…

14 Wars, like revolutions, are judged by the political orders they build, not by what they destroy. Trump is measuring this war by what he has destroyed. History will judge it by its lasting impact on Iran, the Middle East, and the broader global order.

13 Trump wants a quick deal. The regime, for both ideological and structural reasons, cannot make one. So long as the Islamic Republic rules Iran the inevitable outcome is a return to the cold war that predates this conflict and will likely outlast it. nitter.net/ksadjadpour/status/203…


Karim Sadjadpour (@ksadjadpour)

The assassination of Iran's top leaders has inhibited the regime's ability to deliberate and make major decisions, frustrating Trump, who is keen for Tehran to agree to a deal.

12 The most urgent priority isn't Iran's nuclear program—it's the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran is trying to normalize it as its own Panama Canal. This is a problem that should have a diplomatic solution: Europe, Asia, and Arab partners all have a strong interest in keeping it open.

11 History suggests Tehran will overplay its hand. It held American diplomats hostage for 444 days—humiliating the US at the cost of its international standing. It prolonged its ruinous war with Iraq. It praised Hamas's October 7 attack—leading to the destruction of its proxies.

10 One clear lesson from Iraq, Afghanistan, and the Arab Spring is that the US cannot dictate political outcomes. Regime opponents significantly outnumber regime supporters in Iran, but no outside power can forge a new national consensus for Iranians. nytimes.com/2025/06/23/opini…

9 The paradox of the Islamic Republic is that it tends to compromise only under severe pressure, yet that same external pressure and isolation have helped entrench the regime. nytimes.com/2022/08/12/opini…
